note: Driving times are off-peak and only a guide: the Bay Bridge, 101 and Highway 17 can double them. Each trip carries a time from both bases — North Beach and Palo Alto — and the site shows the one nearer to wherever you are. Each says what to do there, in order, and when it is worth going; the ones marked overnight are weekends, not days. Anything with a booking says so. Researched, not yet done — rate them as you go.

items.title: Filoli
items.transit: Drive up Cañada Road, 20 min
items.why: A Georgian Revival house and sixteen acres of formal gardens on 654 acres of the Santa Cruz foothills: a walled garden, an orchard and trails into the nature reserve behind it. It is the nearest real outing from Palo Alto and it changes by season. Autumn Days brings giant pumpkins and cider, and the house is dressed for the holidays from November. Book tickets online.

items.title: Half Moon Bay & the coast
items.transit: Highway 92 over the hill, about 40 min
items.why: The nearest ocean: over the hill on 92 and you are in fog and cypress. Walk the coastal trail and go out to Pillar Point, where the Mavericks surf break sits offshore. Buy fish off the boats in the harbour. In mid-October the town's Art & Pumpkin Festival takes over Main Street and 92 jams all day, so go another weekend.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The Coastal Trail along the bluffs
Pillar Point, looking out at the Mavericks break
Fish straight off the boats at Pillar Point Harbor
Half Moon Bay Brewing on the harbour for the view

items.season: Autumn is the clearest. Avoid the Art & Pumpkin Festival weekend in mid-October unless that is the plan.

items.title: Santa Cruz
items.priceNote: Free to walk; rides and parks extra
items.transit: Highway 17 over the mountains, about 50 min, much longer on summer weekends
items.why: Three kinds of day in one town. There is the Boardwalk, with the 1924 Giant Dipper, one of the oldest wooden roller coasters still running. There is West Cliff Drive, a walk along the cliffs to the surfers at Steamer Lane. And ten minutes inland, the old-growth redwoods of Henry Cowell. Go early: 17 is slow in both directions on a sunny weekend.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The Boardwalk and the 1924 Giant Dipper
West Cliff Drive to Steamer Lane to watch the surfers
Natural Bridges at the end of West Cliff, for tide pools
Henry Cowell redwoods on the way home, ten minutes inland

items.season: All year. Monarch butterflies winter at Natural Bridges from October to February.

items.title: Muir Woods
items.transit: Through San Francisco and over the Golden Gate, about 75 min
items.why: Old-growth coast redwoods in a canyon under Mount Tamalpais, made a national monument in 1908. The flat boardwalk loop is short. Take the Dipsea or Ben Johnson trail up the side of the canyon to get away from the crowd. You cannot just turn up: parking and the shuttle both need a reservation, every day, at gomuirwoods.com.
items.hoursFrom: nps.gov — 8am to around sunset, every day
items.hoursNote: 8am to sunset

stops.text: Reserve parking or the shuttle at gomuirwoods.com first
The boardwalk loop along Redwood Creek
Up the Ben Johnson trail to get away from the crowd
The Pelican Inn at Muir Beach, ten minutes down the road

items.season: All year. Winter brings spawning salmon to Redwood Creek; weekday mornings are quietest.

items.title: Napa Valley
items.transit: About 1h45 via the Bay Bridge or the San Mateo Bridge and I-880
items.why: The valley is thirty miles of vineyards between two ridges, and a good day is two or three wineries, not six. Most tastings are by appointment now, so book them before you drive. Have lunch at the Oxbow Public Market in the town of Napa, and take the Silverado Trail rather than Highway 29 when 29 is jammed. Somebody has to not drink: plan who drives, or stay the night.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours; most wineries want a tasting booked ahead

stops.text: Leave by nine. From the city, over the Golden Gate and through Sonoma, about 75 min
A first tasting at ten or eleven, booked — Yountville or Oakville
Lunch at Oxbow Public Market in Napa, or Oakville Grocery on 29
One more tasting, reached by the Silverado Trail when 29 is jammed
Or finish at the top of the valley in Calistoga, with a mud bath at the hot springs

items.season: Harvest, late August to October, is the best and busiest. January to March is mustard season: yellow between the vines, quiet and cheaper.

items.title: Monterey & Point Lobos
items.transit: US-101 south and Highway 156, about 1h40
items.why: The Monterey Bay Aquarium, on Cannery Row, is the reason to come: the kelp forest tank is three storeys tall. Then go south to Point Lobos, the rockiest, greenest few miles of the coast, where sea otters float in the coves. Point Lobos is moving to reservations for every visitor this year, so check before you go. Carmel is five minutes on and has a card of its own.
items.hoursNote: A day of two places — the aquarium sells timed tickets, and Point Lobos keeps state-park daylight hours

stops.text: Monterey Bay Aquarium when it opens — the kelp forest feeding and the otters first
Lunch on Cannery Row or Fisherman's Wharf
Point Lobos: the Cypress Grove and Sea Lion Point trails — check reservations
Sunset on Carmel Beach, five minutes on

items.season: All year. Autumn is the clearest and warmest on the coast; summer is often foggy.

items.title: Point Reyes
items.transit: Over the Golden Gate and out through Marin, about 2 hours
items.why: A peninsula of cliffs, beaches and cattle ranches. Walk down to the lighthouse, 300-odd steps below the headland. From December to March, elephant seals haul out at Chimney Rock. Tomales Bay oysters, eaten at the water's edge, are the lunch. It is windy and cold out there even when Palo Alto is hot, so bring a layer.
items.hoursFrom: nps.gov — the seashore is open 6am to midnight

stops.text: Hog Island or the Marshall Store on Tomales Bay for oysters at the water
Point Reyes Station, the one-street town, for bread and cheese for the day
Out to the lighthouse and down the 300-odd steps — closed in high wind
Chimney Rock for elephant seals, December to March
Or north to Tomales Point for the tule elk

items.season: All year. Winter has the seals and grey whales; spring the wildflowers on Chimney Rock.

items.title: Big Sur
items.priceNote: Mostly free; state parks ~$10 a car
items.transit: Through Carmel and down Highway 1, about 2h30 to Bixby Bridge
items.why: The drive is the point: Highway 1 on cliffs over the Pacific. Bixby Bridge (1932) is the famous view. At Julia Pfeiffer Burns, McWay Falls drops onto a beach you are not allowed to reach, which somehow makes it better. It is a long day there and back, and better as a night away. The road closes for landslides most winters, so check Caltrans before you set off.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours; check Highway 1 before you set off

stops.text: Bixby Bridge, the famous view, from the turnout on the north side
Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park for a redwood walk and lunch
McWay Falls at Julia Pfeiffer Burns, a short walk from the car park
Sunset from Nepenthe's terrace, then a night in the woods

items.season: Spring and autumn. Winter landslides close Highway 1 most years — check Caltrans before you leave.

items.title: Lake Tahoe
items.priceNote: A weekend: lodging is the cost
items.transit: About 4 hours via I-80 or US-50 — a weekend, not a day
items.why: A clear alpine lake in the Sierra, and a weekend rather than a day. In summer, Emerald Bay and the beaches. In winter, the ski resorts. Friday-evening traffic out of the Bay is the real obstacle, so leave early or on Saturday morning. In winter, chain controls on 80 and 50 are routine: carry chains or have four-wheel drive.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Emerald Bay from the overlook on Highway 89, then down to Vikingsholm
The Rubicon Trail along the shore to D.L. Bliss
Sand Harbor on the Nevada side for the clearest water
In winter: a day at Palisades, Northstar or Heavenly instead

items.season: Summer for the lake, December to April for skiing. Carry chains in winter.

items.title: Yosemite Valley
items.transit: About 4 hours via I-580 and Highway 120 — a weekend, not a day
items.why: Granite walls three thousand feet high: El Capitan, Half Dome, and waterfalls that run hardest in late spring. It needs a weekend. Book somewhere to sleep well ahead, because the valley fills up. The park has used entry reservations at peak times in recent years, so check nps.gov for your dates before you go.
items.hoursFrom: nps.gov — open all day, every day; no entry reservation in 2026

stops.text: Lower Yosemite Fall, a flat mile from the valley floor
The Mist Trail to Vernal Fall — steep, wet, and the best half-day in the park
El Capitan Meadow, looking for climbers on the wall
Tunnel View at sunset
Glacier Point next morning, when the road is open

items.season: Late spring for the waterfalls, autumn for fewer people. Tioga and Glacier Point roads close in winter; check reservations for peak dates.

items.title: Capitola
items.priceNote: Free; parking metered in the village
items.transit: Highway 17 to Santa Cruz, then ten minutes east — about 50 min from Palo Alto
items.why: The nearest thing to the Italian Riviera in California. The Venetian Court is two rows of candy-coloured stucco houses right on the sand, built in 1924 and listed on the National Register. The beach sits in a sheltered cove, so the water is gentler than anywhere else on this coast. It was California's first seaside resort, in 1874. Walk the wharf, eat in the village, and swim if you're brave.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

items.title: Carmel-by-the-Sea
items.transit: US-101 and Highway 1 through Monterey, about 1h45
items.why: A village that looks like an English storybook. In the 1920s Hugh Comstock built fairytale cottages here, with swooping roofs and stone chimneys, and the houses still go by names rather than street numbers. Walk the lanes to find Hansel and Gretel, then down to Carmel Beach: white sand under wind-bent cypress, and dogs off the lead. Pair it with Point Lobos, five minutes south.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

items.title: Sausalito by ferry
items.transit: The ferry from the Ferry Building, about 30 min across the bay
items.why: Go by boat, not by car: the ferry from the Ferry Building crosses the bay past Alcatraz with the Golden Gate on your left. Sausalito is a hillside town over the water. Walk the waterfront, then out to the floating houseboat community on Richardson Bay. Take the ferry back at sunset.
items.hoursNote: The ferry runs to a timetable — goldengate.org/ferry has it

items.title: Año Nuevo elephant seals
items.priceNote: Guided walk + parking, booked ahead in winter
items.transit: Down Highway 1 past Pescadero, about 55 min from Palo Alto
items.why: The largest mainland breeding colony of elephant seals in the world, on a windswept point down the coast. In winter the bulls fight on the beach and the pups are born. From December 15 to March 31 you can only go on a docent-led walk of three to four miles, and those book out, so reserve on ReserveCalifornia the day they open. From April to November you can walk out on your own.
items.hoursNote: The seals are seen on guided walks only, 15 December to 31 March, booked on ReserveCalifornia up to 56 days ahead

items.title: Fitzgerald tide pools
items.transit: Highway 1 to Moss Beach, 15 min north of Half Moon Bay
items.why: Some of the richest tide pooling on the California coast, in Moss Beach. Time it to a low tide of one foot or less, best an hour or two before the lowest point. Then the reef is uncovered and full of giant green anemones, purple sea stars, urchins and hermit crabs, with harbour seals on the rocks. Check a tide table before you go, wear shoes with grip, and bring a jacket. Volunteer naturalists are there at weekends.
items.hoursNote: Opens at 8am every day and closes between 5pm and 8pm with the season; go at low tide

items.title: Solvang and the Santa Ynez Valley
items.transit: US-101 south the whole way, about 4 hours from Palo Alto — a weekend
items.why: A Danish village in the Santa Ynez Valley, founded in 1911 by Danish-Americans who wanted a folk school in the sun: half-timbered houses, windmills, and bakeries selling kringle. It sounds like a theme park and is actually a real town. The valley around it is wine country, the one in the film Sideways, and the reason to stay the night. Pair it with Santa Barbara, forty minutes over the pass.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Æbleskiver from the outdoor window at Solvang Restaurant on Alisal Road
Kringle and a cardamom bun at one of the Copenhagen Drive bakeries
Elverhøj Museum, a Danish farmhouse built by hand — Thursday to Monday, 11 to 5, $5
Mission Santa Inés, founded 1804, at the edge of town
Ten minutes up the road: the tasting rooms of Los Olivos, a one-street town
Sunset in the vineyards on Foxen Canyon Road

items.season: All year. Danish Days, the third weekend of September, is the big one; December brings the Julefest lights. Spring is green and summer is hot inland.

items.title: Paso Robles
items.transit: US-101 south through Salinas, about 2h50 from Palo Alto — a weekend
items.why: Napa before it was Napa: two hundred wineries in the oak hills halfway to Los Angeles, most of them run by the people pouring, and tastings that cost half as much. Go for the reds, the Rhône grapes and the zinfandel. The town square is a proper small-town park ringed with places to eat. Stay a night, because the best thing here happens after dark.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Tin City: a dozen small wineries, a brewery and a cidery in corrugated-iron warehouses — walk between them
Lunch on the downtown square
An afternoon tasting out on Highway 46 West, booked
Sensorio's Field of Light after dark: 58,800 solar-lit glass spheres on a hillside — book the time slot
Next morning, 40 minutes over the hill to the coast at Cambria

items.season: Harvest in September and October is the best time. Summer days are hot, well over 90°F. Winter is quiet and cheaper.
items.imageSubject: Vineyards in the Paso Robles AVA

items.title: Hearst Castle and Cambria
items.priceNote: Grand Rooms tour ~$35; the seals are free
items.transit: US-101 to Paso Robles, then Highway 46 to the coast, about 3h30 — a weekend
items.why: William Randolph Hearst's hilltop palace above the sea, built from 1919 to 1947 and filled with ceilings and choir stalls bought from Spanish monasteries. You can only see it on a tour, and the Grand Rooms tour takes seventy minutes, up about 140 steps. Book it ahead. The coast road below has an elephant seal beach and the pine-wooded village of Cambria for the night.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The Grand Rooms tour: the Assembly Room, the Refectory, the Neptune Pool from above — book up to 60 days ahead
Piedras Blancas, ten minutes north: thousands of elephant seals on the beach below the boardwalk, free
Harmony, pop. 18, for a coffee on the way back
Moonstone Beach boardwalk in Cambria at sunset
Drive home up Highway 1 through Big Sur, if the road is open

items.season: All year. The elephant seal pups are born in January and February, when the beach is fullest. The castle is decorated for the holidays in December.

items.title: Sonoma and Healdsburg
items.transit: Over the Golden Gate and up 101, about an hour to Sonoma from the city
items.why: The easier wine country. The town of Sonoma is built round a leafy plaza where California briefly declared itself a republic in 1846, and the last of the missions stands on one corner. Healdsburg, an hour north, is the other plaza, with the best food in the county and the Russian River and Dry Creek valleys at the end of every street. Do one or the other, not both, and book tastings.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Sonoma Plaza and Mission San Francisco Solano, the last of the 21 missions, 1823
Picnic from the cheese shops on the plaza
One tasting in the Sonoma Valley, booked
Or skip on to Healdsburg: lunch off the plaza, then Dry Creek Valley zinfandel
A swim or a paddle in the Russian River in summer

items.season: Harvest, August to October, is the prettiest and busiest. Spring has the mustard and the wildflowers.

items.title: Mendocino and Fort Bragg
items.priceNote: The headlands are free; the Skunk Train is extra
items.transit: US-101 to Cloverdale, then Highway 128 through Anderson Valley, about 3h15 from the city — a weekend
items.why: A New England fishing village on a headland over the Pacific, with water towers, picket fences and the whole town inside a state park. The drive up is part of it: Highway 128 through the vineyards of Anderson Valley and a redwood tunnel to the sea. Stay two nights. Fort Bragg, ten miles north, has the railway and the glass beach.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Anderson Valley on the way up: apple stands and Alsatian-style wine in Philo
Walk the cliffs of Mendocino Headlands State Park, all around the town
Point Cabrillo Light Station, a mile of path to a lighthouse from 1909
The Skunk Train from Fort Bragg into the redwoods, or the railbikes along Pudding Creek — book ahead
Glass Beach in Fort Bragg: sea-worn glass from an old dump. Look, don't take — it is a state park

items.season: All year. Whales pass from December to April. Summer is foggy on the coast and hot 20 minutes inland.

items.title: Santa Barbara
items.priceNote: Mostly free; the Funk Zone tasting rooms extra
items.transit: US-101 south, about 4h40 from Palo Alto — a weekend, or pair with Solvang
items.why: A Spanish-colonial town between the mountains and the sea, rebuilt in white stucco and red tile after the 1925 earthquake. It is a different California from the Bay: warmer, slower, and in bloom. Climb the courthouse tower, walk the wharf, and spend the evening in the Funk Zone, where the wineries have tasting rooms in old warehouses a block from the beach.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The County Courthouse: free, and the clock tower has the view over the whole town
Old Mission Santa Barbara, "Queen of the Missions", on the hill
Stearns Wharf and the beach path along Cabrillo Boulevard
The Funk Zone at dusk: the Urban Wine Trail, a dozen tasting rooms on foot
Next morning, Solvang for breakfast on the way home

items.season: All year; it is warmer than the Bay in every month. June is cool and grey here too.

items.title: Pinnacles National Park
items.transit: US-101 to Gilroy, then Highway 25 to the east entrance, about 1h45
items.why: The remains of an ancient volcano, torn in half by the San Andreas Fault: rock spires, talus caves you walk through with a torch, and California condors riding the thermals overhead. It is the nearest national park and the least visited. It is too hot in summer; go between October and May. Use the east entrance, because the two sides do not connect by road.
items.hoursNote: Open all day — the east entrance is the one for the caves and the High Peaks

stops.text: Start early at the east entrance; the Bear Gulch lot fills by ten at weekends
Bear Gulch Cave: a scramble through boulders in the dark — bring a torch, and check it is open (it closes for bats)
Bear Gulch Reservoir, above the cave
The High Peaks trail: steps cut into the rock and handrails, and the best chance of condors
Home via Hollister, or the fruit stands on 25 in summer

items.season: October to May. Spring brings wildflowers; summer is regularly over 100°F. Check the cave status on nps.gov before you go.

items.title: Angel Island
items.transit: Golden Gate Ferry from the Ferry Building, about 30 min — or the short ferry from Tiburon
items.why: The biggest island in the bay, a state park you can only reach by boat. A five-mile road loops round it with a view of the Golden Gate, the city, Alcatraz and Mount Tam in turn. On the far side is the Immigration Station, where from 1910 to 1940 Chinese immigrants were held, sometimes for months, and carved poems into the barracks walls. They are still there. Check the ferry times first: there are only a few sailings a day.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Ferry to Ayala Cove — from the Ferry Building, or from Tiburon
Walk or cycle the Perimeter Road, 5 miles, with the whole bay in turn
The Immigration Station and its poems, on the north-east side
Or climb Mount Livermore, 788 feet, for the view from the middle of the bay
Picnic back at Ayala Cove before the last boat

items.season: All year, weekends especially. The Blue & Gold boat from Pier 41 is suspended in 2026, so use the Ferry Building or Tiburon.
